thread.title: Wake Forest expands leadership in neuroarts with new lab focused on health benefits
thread.title_full: Wake Forest expands leadership in neuroarts with new lab focused on health benefits

author: l. m. sharp
title: Wake Forest expands leadership in neuroarts with new lab focused on health benefits
text:
Wake Forest University is expanding its role in the field of neuroarts, a discipline that studies how creative activities can support brain health and overall well-being. In January 2026, the university launched a Neuroarts Lab as part of the global NeuroArts Blueprint Initiative, which aims to integrate arts into mainstream medical practices.
On February 13, more than 30 presenters and participants gathered at the Intergenerational Center for Arts and Wellness in Winston-Salem for a symposium focused on the intersection of neuroscience and the arts. The event brought together artists, scholars, clinicians, service organizations, community members, and funders to discuss how creative expression can aid medical recovery and cognitive health.
Kimberley McAllister, vice provost for research at Wake Forest University, highlighted the significance of this multidisciplinary approach: “There are three pillars to understanding how brain function impacts society – neurohealth, neuroarts and neurohumanities,” McAllister said. “Neuroarts is where science meets the soul, and it’s an area Wake Forest has pioneered in the world with a dance and dementia program where artists and scientists work together.”
The new Neuroarts Lab focuses on research showing that engaging in artistic activities can measurably change brain function, body responses, and behavior to improve health outcomes. Dr. David Popoli from Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist described neuroarts as essential for both physical and cognitive rehabilitation. He noted that by bridging artistic language with clinical practice—such as understanding dance terms alongside medical terminology—healthcare providers can treat activities like museum visits or dance classes with similar importance as traditional therapy sessions.
One initiative discussed was Arts Rx—a program where healthcare providers prescribe arts-based activities such as concerts or pottery classes to improve patients’ mental and physical well-being. Aly Maier Lokuta from New Jersey Performing Arts Center emphasized patient-centered care: “To offer social and cultural prescriptions, we need to ask patients, ‘What brings you joy?’” Lokuta explained that after receiving an arts prescription, patients are supported by connectors who help them find suitable activities based on their interests or needs.
Dr. Kathryn Callahan from Wake Forest Baptist Health pointed out potential benefits for older adults: “Older adults may experience a loss of identity or loss of purpose when the labels they ascribed to themselves are threatened,” she said. “Thriving in older age means having a sense of purpose and creating new labels for themselves by re-engaging in fun.”
The university’s efforts build on over ten years of faculty innovation led by professors Christina Soriano (dance) and Christina Hugenschmidt (gerontology). In 2023, Wake Forest University received a $3 million grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to study how different aspects of dance impact fitness, memory, and brain health through a project called IGROOVE.
Dr. Hugenschmidt commented on these developments: “The institutional investment in the Wake Forest Neuroarts Lab adds momentum to the incredible expansion of research and collaborations happening in Winston-Salem, Charlotte and across the state,” she said. “We are excited to initiate new projects and collaborations that will change the narrative around scholarly research and creative work, making both more accessible to our community.”
The Intergenerational Center for Arts & Wellness serves as headquarters for Senior Services Inc., located near Shorefair Drive in Winston-Salem. Its central location makes it accessible for over 20 collaborating organizations running programs there.
Lokuta outlined future goals: “If we want the arts to be a true partner in healthcare, we have to make it as easy for a doctor to prescribe a museum visit as it is for them to prescribe an antibiotic,” she said. “We are working toward a future where that ‘warm handover’ doesn’t just happen via a phone call with a link worker but is built into the digital fabric of the healthcare system – ensuring that every patient, regardless of their zip code, has a clear path to the healing power of culture.”

One initiative discussed was Arts Rx—a program where healthcare providers prescribe arts-based activities such as concerts or pottery classes to improve patients’ mental and physical well-being.
